title: 12. Cloud, Containers & Deployment: Cloud Providers (AWS vs Azure vs GCP)
summary: Cloud providers are the public-cloud platforms — led by Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP) — that rent compute, storage, network, and higher-level managed services on demand, with each…
objectives: What are the main differences between AWS, Azure, and GCP, and how do you choose between them?
How do the pricing models differ, and what discount mechanisms should a team use?
What is multi-cloud, and when does it make sense?
How do AWS, Azure, and GCP compare for data analytics and machine learning?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Cloud providers are the public-cloud platforms — led by Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP) — that rent compute, storage, network, and higher-level managed services on demand, with each provider offering a distinct catalog, pricing model, ecosystem, and set of strengths that make one a better fit than another for a given workload.
The public cloud market is dominated by three providers — AWS, Azure, and GCP — which together hold roughly two-thirds of the global market and define the vocabulary of modern infrastructure. Each has a distinct heritage that shapes its strengths. AWS launched in 2006 with S3 and EC2, predating its competitors by four years, and used that head start to build the broadest service catalog (200+ services), the largest partner ecosystem, and the deepest operational maturity. Azure launched in 2010 from Microsoft's enterprise software business, and inherited Microsoft's existing relationships with Fortune 500 companies — every enterprise already had a Microsoft enterprise agreement, Active Directory, and Windows Server, so Azure was the path of least resistance for hybrid scenarios. GCP launched in 2008 (App Engine) and re-launched in 2012 with Compute Engine, building on Google's internal infrastructure (Borg, the predecessor to Kubernetes; Bigtable, the predecessor to BigQuery; and the global fiber network that powers Search and YouTube) — so GCP's strengths are data analytics, machine learning, and a planet-scale network. The choice between them is rarely "which is best" and almost always "which is best for this workload, this team, and this organization."

The first concept is market share and momentum. As of 2024, AWS holds roughly 31% of the global cloud market, Azure about 24% (and growing fastest), and GCP about 11%. AWS's lead is shrinking slowly as Azure and GCP grow faster, but AWS's absolute revenue continues to increase — the market is growing for everyone. The remaining ~34% is split among Alibaba Cloud, Oracle Cloud, IBM Cloud, and dozens of regional providers. AWS's dominance is most pronounced in North American startups and internet companies; Azure's growth is driven by enterprise migrations (Microsoft's existing customer base moving from on-prem Windows Server / SQL Server to Azure); GCP's footprint is concentrated in data-heavy companies (Snapchat, Spotify, PayPal) and AI/ML workloads. Market share matters because it drives the ecosystem: AWS has the most third-party tooling, the most certified engineers, and the most reference architectures; Azure has the deepest enterprise integrations; GCP has the strongest data and ML community. A team choosing a cloud should consider not just the services but the ecosystem they will operate within.

The second concept is the service catalog and its overlaps. All three providers offer the foundational services — virtual machines (EC2 / Azure VM / Compute Engine), object storage (S3 / Blob Storage / Cloud Storage), block storage (EBS / Managed Disks / Persistent Disk), virtual networks (VPC / VNet / VPC), managed databases (RDS / Azure SQL / Cloud SQL), and load balancers — and these are largely interchangeable. The differentiation is in higher-level services. AWS leads in breadth: Lambda (serverless, launched 2014 and still the most mature), DynamoDB (managed NoSQL with single-digit-millisecond latency at any scale), Aurora (MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible with multi-region replication), SQS/SNS/Kinesis (messaging and streaming), and Fargate (serverless containers). Azure leads in enterprise integration: Active Directory (the identity standard for enterprises), Azure Stack (on-premises Azure for hybrid), Windows VMs and SQL Server images with built-in licensing, and Power Platform integration. GCP leads in data and ML: BigQuery (serverless data warehouse, the best-in-class for analytics), Cloud Spanner (globally-distributed SQL database with external consistency), Vertex AI (managed ML platform with AutoML, custom training, and model registry), and TensorFlow (Google's framework, with first-class GCP support). Choosing a cloud often starts with one differentiating service: a team that needs BigQuery picks GCP; a team that needs tight Active Directory integration picks Azure; a team that needs the broadest catalog picks AWS.

The third concept is the network and global footprint. AWS has the most regions (33+ launched, with more announced), giving the lowest latency to the most users and the most options for data residency (a German company can keep data in eu-central-1, an Indian company in ap-south-1). Azure has a comparable region count (60+ "regions," though many are availability-zone equivalents within a larger area) and the most certifications for compliance (FedRAMP, HIPAA, EU GDPR, China, government clouds). GCP has fewer regions (35+) but the best inter-region network: Google's private global fiber backbone carries traffic between regions without touching the public internet, with the lowest latency between continents and the best support for global load balancing (a single anycast IP routes to the nearest healthy region). For a globally-distributed service where cross-region latency matters (a globally consistent database, a global anycast API), GCP's network is a meaningful advantage. For a service that must operate in many specific countries (data residency, regulatory compliance), AWS's region count is a meaningful advantage. For an enterprise migrating from on-prem with existing Microsoft infrastructure, Azure's hybrid connectivity (ExpressRoute, Azure Stack) is a meaningful advantage.

The fourth concept is the pricing model. All three charge by consumption (per-second compute, per-GB storage, per-GB network egress), and at the list-price level they are within 5–10% of each other for comparable services. The differences are in the discount mechanisms. AWS offers Reserved Instances (1- or 3-year commitments for a 30–75% discount), Savings Plans (commit to a $/hour spend for a similar discount, more flexible than RIs), and Spot Instances (up to 90% discount for interruptible capacity). Azure offers Reserved VM Instances (similar to AWS RIs), Azure Hybrid Benefit (use existing on-prem Windows Server and SQL Server licenses, up to 85% savings — a unique Azure advantage for enterprises), and Spot VMs. GCP offers Committed Use Discounts (1- or 3-year, automatically applied, no upfront payment), Sustained Use Discounts (automatic discount for running a VM more than 25% of a month, up to 30% — a unique GCP advantage), and Preemptible VMs / Spot VMs. The pricing model that fits depends on the workload: enterprises with existing Microsoft licenses should choose Azure for the Hybrid Benefit; startups with spiky workloads benefit from GCP's per-second billing and Sustained Use Discounts; teams that want to commit for discounts but need flexibility should compare AWS Savings Plans to GCP Committed Use Discounts. Egress charges are a hidden cost: all three charge for data leaving the cloud (e.g., $0.09/GB from AWS to internet), and multi-cloud architectures that move data between clouds incur egress on both sides.

The fifth concept is the real-world customer patterns. Netflix is the canonical AWS-only customer: Netflix's entire streaming infrastructure runs on AWS (everything except the content delivery network, which Netflix built itself), and Netflix's architecture (microservices, Chaos Monkey, multi-region active-active) is the reference design for AWS-native systems. Microsoft runs its own consumer services (Office 365, Xbox Live, Bing, LinkedIn) on Azure, demonstrating Azure's scalability for high-traffic workloads. Snapchat moved from Google App Engine to GCP for its full stack, citing GCP's data infrastructure (BigQuery for analytics) and global network as decisive; Spotify moved from on-prem to GCP for similar reasons, particularly BigQuery. Many companies run multi-cloud: Airbnb uses AWS for compute and GCP for BigQuery analytics; PayPal uses GCP for ML and Azure for enterprise workloads; Apple uses both AWS and GCP for iCloud storage. The pattern is: pure-cloud is simpler operationally (one set of tools, one IAM model, one billing); multi-cloud is more complex but lets each workload use the best service for its needs (often AWS for general compute, GCP for data/ML, Azure for enterprise). Multi-cloud is rarely a single application running across clouds; it is usually different applications or different layers (compute vs analytics) on different clouds, connected by data pipelines.

The sixth concept is the trade-off summary and the decision framework. AWS is the default for breadth: the largest service catalog, the largest ecosystem, the most certified engineers, the most reference architectures; choose AWS when you need breadth, when your team is already familiar with it, or when you want the lowest risk of hitting a service gap. Azure is the default for Microsoft enterprises: the deepest integration with Active Directory, Windows Server, SQL Server, and Office 365; the best hybrid cloud (Azure Stack); and the best government clouds (FedRAMP High, Azure Government); choose Azure when you are a Microsoft shop, when you need hybrid, or when you are in regulated industries. GCP is the default for data and AI: BigQuery is the best-in-class data warehouse, Vertex AI and TensorFlow are the best-in-class ML platform, the global network is the best for globally-distributed services; choose GCP when data analytics or ML is central to your product, when you need a globally consistent database (Spanner), or when you want the best price-performance for stateless compute (per-second billing, Sustained Use Discounts). The decision is rarely "which is best" and almost always "which is best for this workload" — many organizations use all three, picking the right tool for each layer of their stack.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Cloud provider selector.
- Description of the workload to be placed on a cloud.
- Score each cloud against the workload and recommend the best fit.
- ML / AI workloads favor GCP (Vertex AI, TensorFlow).
- Large-scale analytics favor GCP (BigQuery).
- Globally consistent SQL favors GCP (Spanner).
- Breadth of services favors AWS.
- Microsoft shop / hybrid / government cloud favor Azure.

**Defines:** `Workload`, `CloudScore`, `CloudSelector`

```python
"""
Cloud provider selector.

Given a workload's requirements, picks the best-fit cloud provider
(AWS / Azure / GCP) based on weighted scoring across categories:
- service fit (does the cloud have best-in-class for the workload?)
- enterprise integration (Microsoft shop? hybrid? compliance?)
- cost model (discounts applicable to the workload pattern?)
- team expertise (existing familiarity reduces operating cost)
- region coverage (data residency and global latency needs)

This is the decision model an architect uses; it does not call
cloud APIs but encodes the trade-offs.
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Dict, List

@dataclass
class Workload:
    """Description of the workload to be placed on a cloud."""
    name: str
    needs_ml: bool = False               # ML / AI central to product
    needs_analytics: bool = False        # large-scale data warehouse
    needs_global_sql: bool = False       # globally consistent SQL DB
    microsoft_shop: bool = False         # existing AD / Windows / SQL Server
    needs_hybrid: bool = False           # on-prem + cloud integration
    needs_gov_cloud: bool = False        # regulatory / compliance cloud
    needs_breadth: bool = False          # many different service types
    steady_state_compute: bool = False   # always-on, predictable VM usage
    has_ms_licenses: bool = False        # existing Windows/SQL Server licenses
    spiky_workload: bool = False         # bursty, interruptible OK
    data_residency_countries: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    team_expertise: Dict[str, int] = field(default_factory=lambda: {
        "aws": 1, "azure": 1, "gcp": 1})  # 1-5 familiarity per cloud

@dataclass
class CloudScore:
    provider: str
    score: float
    rationale: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)

class CloudSelector:
    """Score each cloud against the workload and recommend the best fit."""

    PROVIDERS = ["aws", "azure", "gcp"]

    def score(self, w: Workload) -> List[CloudScore]:
        scores = {p: CloudScore(p, 50.0) for p in self.PROVIDERS}
        self._score_service_fit(w, scores)
        self._score_enterprise(w, scores)
        self._score_cost(w, scores)
        self._score_expertise(w, scores)
        self._score_regions(w, scores)
        return sorted(scores.values(), key=lambda s: -s.score)

    def _score_service_fit(self, w: Workload, scores: Dict[str, CloudScore]) -> None:
        # ML / AI workloads favor GCP (Vertex AI, TensorFlow).
        if w.needs_ml:
            scores["gcp"].score += 15
            scores["gcp"].rationale.append("Vertex AI + TensorFlow best-in-class for ML")
            scores["aws"].score += 5
            scores["aws"].rationale.append("SageMaker solid but not best-in-class")
        # Large-scale analytics favor GCP (BigQuery).
        if w.needs_analytics:
            scores["gcp"].score += 15
            scores["gcp"].rationale.append("BigQuery best-in-class for analytics")
            scores["aws"].score += 5
            scores["aws"].rationale.append("Redshift + Athena competent")
        # Globally consistent SQL favors GCP (Spanner).
        if w.needs_global_sql:
            scores["gcp"].score += 10
            scores["gcp"].rationale.append("Spanner offers external consistency")
            scores["azure"].score += 3
            scores["azure"].rationale.append("Cosmos DB multi-master is solid")
        # Breadth of services favors AWS.
        if w.needs_breadth:
            scores["aws"].score += 15
            scores["aws"].rationale.append("200+ services, broadest catalog")
            scores["azure"].score += 5
            scores["azure"].rationale.append("Second-broadest catalog")

    def _score_enterprise(self, w: Workload, scores: Dict[str, CloudScore]) -> None:
        # Microsoft shop / hybrid / government cloud favor Azure.
        if w.microsoft_shop:
            scores["azure"].score += 20
            scores["azure"].rationale.append("Native AD / Windows / SQL Server integration")
            scores["aws"].score -= 5
            scores["aws"].rationale.append("Requires AD Connector or standalone AD")
        if w.needs_hybrid:
            scores["azure"].score += 15
            scores["azure"].rationale.append("Azure Stack enables true hybrid")
        if w.needs_gov_cloud:
            scores["azure"].score += 10
            scores["azure"].rationale.append("Azure Government most certified (FedRAMP High)")
            scores["aws"].score += 5
            scores["aws"].rationale.append("AWS GovCloud competent")

    def _score_cost(self, w: Workload, scores: Dict[str, CloudScore]) -> None:
        # Existing Microsoft licenses favor Azure (Hybrid Benefit).
        if w.has_ms_licenses:
            scores["azure"].score += 15
            scores["azure"].rationale.append("Azure Hybrid Benefit reuses licenses (up to 85% off)")
        # Steady-state compute favors GCP (Sustained Use Discount, automatic).
        if w.steady_state_compute:
            scores["gcp"].score += 8
            scores["gcp"].rationale.append("Sustained Use Discounts automatic (up to 30%)")
            scores["aws"].score += 3
            scores["aws"].rationale.append("Savings Plans need commitment")
        # Spiky / interruptible favors Spot on any cloud, slight GCP edge.
        if w.spiky_workload:
            scores["gcp"].score += 5
            scores["gcp"].rationale.append("Per-second billing, Preemptible VMs (up to 80% off)")
            scores["aws"].score += 4
            scores["aws"].rationale.append("Spot Instances (up to 90% off)")

    def _score_expertise(self, w: Workload, scores: Dict[str, CloudScore]) -> None:
        # Team familiarity reduces operating cost and time-to-production.
        for p in self.PROVIDERS:
            exp = w.team_expertise.get(p, 1)
            bonus = (exp - 1) * 4  # 0 to 16 points
            if bonus > 0:
                scores[p].score += bonus
                scores[p].rationale.append(f"Team familiarity {exp}/5 (+{bonus})")

    def _score_regions(self, w: Workload, scores: Dict[str, CloudScore]) -> None:
        # Many data-residency countries favor AWS (most regions).
        n = len(w.data_residency_countries)
        if n >= 3:
            scores["aws"].score += 8
            scores["aws"].rationale.append(f"Most regions (33+), good for {n} countries")
            scores["azure"].score += 6
            scores["azure"].rationale.append("60+ regions, strong coverage")
        elif n > 0:
            scores["aws"].score += 3
            scores["azure"].score += 3

    def recommend(self, w: Workload) -> CloudScore:
        ranked = self.score(w)
        return ranked[0]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    selector = CloudSelector()

    # Case 1: AI/ML startup building a recommendation engine.
    ml_startup = Workload(
        name="AI recommendation engine",
        needs_ml=True, needs_analytics=True, spiky_workload=True,
        team_expertise={"aws": 3, "azure": 1, "gcp": 4},
    )
    print(f"== {ml_startup.name} ==")
    for s in selector.score(ml_startup):
        print(f"  {s.provider:>5}: {s.score:>5.1f}  ({'; '.join(s.rationale[:2])})")
    rec = selector.recommend(ml_startup)
    print(f"  -> recommend: {rec.provider}\n")

    # Case 2: Fortune 500 Microsoft shop migrating on-prem apps.
    enterprise = Workload(
        name="Enterprise Microsoft migration",
        microsoft_shop=True, needs_hybrid=True, has_ms_licenses=True,
        needs_gov_cloud=True,
        team_expertise={"aws": 1, "azure": 5, "gcp": 1},
    )
    print(f"== {enterprise.name} ==")
    for s in selector.score(enterprise):
        print(f"  {s.provider:>5}: {s.score:>5.1f}  ({'; '.join(s.rationale[:2])})")
    rec = selector.recommend(enterprise)
    print(f"  -> recommend: {rec.provider}\n")

    # Case 3: General-purpose SaaS needing broadest catalog.
    saas = Workload(
        name="General SaaS platform",
        needs_breadth=True, steady_state_compute=True,
        data_residency_countries=["US", "EU", "Brazil", "India"],
        team_expertise={"aws": 4, "azure": 2, "gcp": 2},
    )
    print(f"== {saas.name} ==")
    for s in selector.score(saas):
        print(f"  {s.provider:>5}: {s.score:>5.1f}  ({'; '.join(s.rationale[:2])})")
    rec = selector.recommend(saas)
    print(f"  -> recommend: {rec.provider}")
```
